newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa rightist gets 6 years for beating blacks.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa rightist gets 6 years for beating blacks.

text.p: South African white supremacist Eugene Terre Blanche was sentenced to six years in jail on Tuesday for trying to murder a black man.
Terre Blanche, 53, was granted bail pending an appeal but had to wait some three hours before being freed after supporters brought sacks of coins to court to pay his bail.

The right-winger was sentenced to six years in prison for attempting to murder former employee Paul Motshabi, 27. The victim suffered severe brain damage when Terre Blanche beat him in March last year.
Magistrate Chris Eksteen also sentenced Terre Blanche to one year in jail for the serious assault of John Ndzima last November. He ruled that the two terms be served concurrently.

Terre Blanche, leader of the neo-Nazi Afrikaner Resistance Movement (AWB), was given permission to lodge a high court appeal against the sentence and conviction and granted bail of 20,000 rand ($4,450). He was ordered not to leave South Africa.
The grey-bearded rightist sat impassively in the court in Potchefstroom, southwest of Johannesburg, and his supporters remained subdued as he stood to hear the magistrate pronounce sentence.

"It's the greatest injustice. I regard it as laughable. I am convinced the appeal case will prove me correct. If I should go to prison today, the truth would then be locked in with me," he later told reporters while waiting for bail to be posted.
The magistrate and court officials became visibly annoyed when AWB members handed in bags of coins as bail payment, and sent Terre Blanche down to the cells while the money was counted.

The AWB leader was later transported to the local prison to await payment of the full amount when it became clear that not enough had been raised amongst his supporters. The balance was eventually covered by a bank guaranteed cheque and cash notes.
Earlier, magistrate Eksteen said Terre Blanche had shown no remorse for his crimes and banned him from owning any firearms.
Police had sealed off the courthouse with razor-wire and used dogs to drive back a group of several hundred blacks singing and waving placards demanding that the rightwing leader be jailed for life.

Terre Blanche rallied thousands of rightists behind his cause during talks to end apartheid in the early 1990s, but his support has waned under South Africa's peaceful transition to majority rule, instead of the bloodbath he had forecast.
Terre Blanche, a gruff-voiced farmer and poet, styled himself on Boer heroes who fought British colonialism at the turn of the last century.
In 1992, he became an object of ridicule after falling off his horse at a neo-Nazi style gathering in Pretoria.

His AWB, a movement of gun-toting rightists sporting khaki uniforms with swastika-style logos, suffered a humiliating blow in 1994 when members tried to prop up an unpopular black leader in the apartheid-created Bophuthatswana homeland.

Their aim was to help the homeland leader resist pressure to take part in South Africa's first all-race elections, but the campaign ended in about 50 deaths -- among them two right-wingers shot dead by a homeland soldier as they begged for mercy.
Terre Blanche hailed the episode as a "brilliant victory".
Political analysts disagreed, saying it was a sign that the movement simply comprised paunchy "brandy and Coke" militants.

Nelson Mandela's African National Congress, which took power in the 1994 elections, said in a statement on Tuesday the magistrate's ruling was a "good signal to the communities that no one is above the law". ($1=4.50 rand)
